section_summary: This section consists chiefly of cross-reference sheets, correspondence, diplomatic despatches, telegrams, legal memoranda, export statistics, and press reports concerning arms, ammunition, aircraft, fuel, and other strategic materials supplied to Japan and China during the Manchurian and Shanghai crises. State Department officials repeatedly concluded that the Executive lacked authority to embargo private arms exports to Japan without congressional authorization and generally declined either to approve or disapprove proposed sales. Later documents track British, French, German, Polish, Czechoslovak, and American shipments and record Chinese objections that an embargo applied equally to China and Japan would favor Japanese aggression.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Sperry Gyroscope ordnance exports
subfiles.about: Records a Navy Department opinion concerning possible prevention of Sperry Gyroscope Company exports to the Japanese Government.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: a Navy letter on proposed ordnance exports to Japan and a Judge Advocate General opinion on using 50 USC 32 to stop it (Sperry Gyroscope).

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on American blanket sales to China and Japan
subfiles.about: Summarizes a request for government help selling Army blankets to the Chinese and Japanese Governments.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: an American blanket manufacturer sought attaché help in Shanghai and Tokyo; the Department opposed special assistance, noting munitions export rules for China.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Elmer Thomas's munitions inquiry
subfiles.about: Records an inquiry about whether Japan or China was obtaining munitions from the United States.
subfiles.summary: The note cross-references Senator Elmer Thomas's letter. His question concerned the procurement of American munitions by both Asian powers.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on shipments of munitions to Japan
subfiles.about: Records a request for information about munitions shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Second cross-reference to Senator Elmer Thomas's correspondence on American munitions shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on exports of war materials to China and Japan
subfiles.about: References a military attaché report on the exportation of war materials to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Parker's report from Britain on exports of war matériel to China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Letter requesting the Department's attitude toward selling military aircraft to Japan
subfiles.about: Asks whether the State Department objects to a possible private sale of military aircraft to the Japanese Government.
subfiles.summary: Barnes asks the Department's attitude toward selling military aircraft to Japan, holding plans until it answers to avoid embarrassing relations in the Far East.

subfiles.title: Routing memorandum transmitting the approved Barnes reply
subfiles.about: Forwards the approved reply to Baron G. Barnes and notes deletion of other divisional routing.
subfiles.summary: Routing memo attaching the approved Barnes reply; Hornbeck cut circulation to save time.

subfiles.title: Reply on the legality of military-aircraft sales to Japan
subfiles.about: Explains that military aircraft may legally be sold to Japan and that the Department neither approves nor objects to the project.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck states that the Department's export-control authority is limited to presidential proclamations issued under the Joint Resolution of January 31, 1922. Because those measures did not prohibit sales to Japan, the proposed transaction was legal. The Department nevertheless declined to express either approval or disapproval.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on House Joint Resolution 137
subfiles.from: J. Charles Linthicum, Committee on Foreign Affairs
subfiles.about: References a letter enclosing Hamilton Fish's resolution to prohibit arms exports to belligerent nations.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to House Joint Resolution 137 (Fish), which would prohibit arms exports to belligerents.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on possible policy toward arms sales to Japan
subfiles.from: Office of the Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Considers whether the Department should announce a policy discouraging American arms transactions with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Memo contrasts licensing arms for civil-war China with non-encouragement toward other states, and asks whether to make a comparable statement on sales to Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Senator Dill's proposed China-Japan arms embargo
subfiles.about: Summarizes Senator Dill's joint resolution prohibiting arms and munitions sales or exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Senator Dill's China-Japan arms embargo resolution was referred to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

subfiles.title: Letter asking Stimson's position on an arms embargo
subfiles.about: Asks whether Stimson supports an embargo and whether the State Department can halt war-goods shipments without Congress.
subfiles.summary: Durham asks Stimson's position on an arms embargo and whether the Department can act alone or must await Congress.

subfiles.title: Reply to Durham concerning statutory arms-export authority
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains that the State Department's authority over arms exports is confined to the 1922 joint resolution and its proclamations.
subfiles.summary: Reply cites 1922, 1924 and 1926 presidential proclamations to show the limited statutory basis for controlling arms exports.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Honduran mahogany for Japanese propellers
subfiles.about: References a purchase of Honduran mahogany for airplane-propeller manufacture in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: about 50,000 square feet of Honduran mahogany due at Vancouver in spring 1932, for Japanese aircraft propellers.

subfiles.title: Descriptive entry for Senate Joint Resolution 89
subfiles.about: Describes Senator Dill's resolution to prohibit arms and munitions exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Entry for Senate Joint Resolution 89 (January 26, 1932), proposing an arms embargo on both China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on aviation-gasoline sales
subfiles.about: Records that American companies would not be asked to stop selling gasoline to either Chinese or Japanese buyers.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: no request would be made that American firms refrain from aviation gasoline sales, a policy applied equally to China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on the British view of gasoline sales
subfiles.about: Records the British Ambassador's approval of the Shanghai consul general's position on aviation-gasoline sales.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: the British Ambassador thought the consul general's stance on gasoline sales to the Chinese military correct.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Far Eastern demand for Polish industry
subfiles.about: References a despatch about increased Polish textile and munitions activity caused by Far Eastern fighting.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: press reports of Polish textile orders for Chinese and Japanese forces and alleged arms orders, with a despatch and clippings.

subfiles.title: Despatch on Polish textile and arms orders for the Far East
subfiles.from: Leon Dominian, American Consul General at Stuttgart
subfiles.about: Transmits German press reports alleging increased Polish textile production and large Japanese arms orders.
subfiles.summary: Dominian encloses reports from the Badische Presse claiming that Łódź textile firms were receiving substantial orders for Chinese and Japanese troops. The articles say major mills had increased working schedules and that some French cotton mills had also received military orders. A separate Moscow report alleges that Japan placed arms and ammunition orders worth several million dollars with Polish firms.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on communist attacks and ammunition transit through Hamburg
subfiles.about: References a report that communists accused Czechoslovakia of sending ammunition to Japan through Hamburg.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: the Volkszeitung alleged Czechoslovak ammunition was moving via Hamburg for Japan, context for attacks on consulates.

subfiles.title: Despatch on attacks against Japanese and Czechoslovak consulates in Hamburg
subfiles.from: John Kehl, American Consul General at Hamburg
subfiles.about: Reports communist stone-throwing attacks on Japanese and Czechoslovak consular offices.
subfiles.summary: Despatch: about twenty demonstrators attacked the Japanese Consulate General in Hamburg and cyclists broke Czechoslovak Consulate windows, amid communist denunciations of Japan and ammunition allegations; police protection increased.

subfiles.title: Legal memorandum on executive authority to prohibit arms exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Concludes that the Executive cannot prohibit private arms exports to Japan in peacetime without congressional authorization.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reviews the 1911 commerce treaty with Japan, the 1922 joint resolution, American neutrality doctrine, and earlier Attorney General opinions. It concludes that existing embargo authority applies only to domestic violence in American countries or countries where the United States exercises extraterritorial jurisdiction. It further observes that China and Japan had not formally declared war and argues that a Japan-specific embargo could be considered unfriendly or an unequal change in neutrality law.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on rumored arms ship off California
subfiles.about: Records an unconfirmed rumor of a vessel carrying arms and ammunition to Japan off the California coast.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: an unconfirmed rumor of an arms-laden ship bound for Japan off Lower California.

subfiles.title: Descriptive entry for 1931 American war-material exports
subfiles.from: Department of Commerce, Iron and Steel Division
subfiles.about: Identifies a Commerce Department list of American war-material exports to Japan and China during 1931.
subfiles.summary: Entry for Iron and Steel Division statistics on 1931 US war-material exports to Japan and China.

subfiles.title: Descriptive entry for January 1932 American war-supply exports
subfiles.from: Department of Commerce, Iron and Steel Division
subfiles.about: Identifies a list of American war-supply exports to Japan and China during January 1932.
subfiles.summary: Entry for Commerce Iron and Steel Division statistics on January 1932 war-supply exports to China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on War Department inquiry about Japanese purchases
subfiles.about: Records a request for the State Department's attitude toward American business sales of war matériel to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Secretary of War Hurley asked guidance on private American sales to Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on arms-export data for Japan
subfiles.about: References a memorandum providing data on American exports of arms and ammunition to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Bundy's information on the volume of US arms and ammunition sent to Japan.

subfiles.title: Commerce Department letter and statement on exports to Japan and China
subfiles.about: Supplies statistics rebutting a claim that the United States had shipped $180 million in munitions to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Commerce shows only $147,212 in war materials went to Japan in 1931 and $58,756 in early 1932, mostly aircraft engines, plus large cotton and linters shipments.

subfiles.title: Letter correcting a British journal's claim about American munitions exports
subfiles.about: Explains the origin and apparent inaccuracy of a claim that $180 million in munitions had been shipped to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck says he found no such House declaration, tracing the claim to Judge Linebarger's testimony apparently from a Chinese newspaper, and invites Atherton to tell the New Statesman.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on James A. McGuire arms investigation
subfiles.about: References a closed investigation of James A. McGuire's alleged arms and munitions sales to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: A Justice Department special agent investigated McGuire's activities. The note reports that the case had been marked closed.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on British export permits for Japan
subfiles.about: References figures for British war matériel licensed for export to Japan from November 1931 through April 1932.
subfiles.summary: The note points to Atherton's despatch transmitting official British information. The statistics cover export permits issued over a six-month period.

subfiles.title: Despatch and parliamentary record of British war-material exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Ray Atherton, for the American Ambassador in London
subfiles.about: Transmits a House of Commons statement listing British war matériel licensed for export to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The parliamentary answer lists machine guns, cartridges, artillery, armored vehicles, aircraft gun mountings, projectiles, and related equipment licensed between November 1931 and April 1932. The Board of Trade disclosed quantities but declined to publish values. The heaviest listed activity occurred in February and March 1932.

subfiles.title: War Department letter about a proposed Japanese crude-oil purchase
subfiles.about: Requests advice on answering an inquiry about a Japanese firm's proposed purchase of American crude oil.
subfiles.summary: Secretary Hurley received a letter on a proposed Japanese crude-oil purchase; Thompson asks Hornbeck how to respond.

subfiles.title: Internal routing note on the Campbell oil inquiry
subfiles.about: Routes a proposed response concerning the Campbell crude-oil inquiry for approval.
subfiles.summary: Partly illegible note asking Rogers to review handling of the Campbell oil inquiry, referring to a Hornbeck suggestion.

subfiles.title: Reply on the proposed sale of crude oil to a Japanese firm
subfiles.about: States that the State Department finds no basis for intervention in a private crude-oil sale to a Japanese firm.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck says the Department appreciates being informed but ordinarily expresses neither approval nor disapproval of such transactions. He notes that the Navy Department has shown substantial interest in Japanese governmental and commercial purchases of crude oil. He assumes that Campbell's information will be shared with the Navy.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese purchases of war matériel
subfiles.about: References War Department correspondence concerning Japan's purchase of war matériel.
subfiles.summary: The brief entry identifies a letter filed elsewhere. Its sole recorded subject is the purchase of military supplies by Japan.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck memorandum on the proposed Franklin-engine reply
subfiles.about: Approves a proposed War Department reply about Franklin engines but recommends removing any governmental endorsement.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck accepts Burnett's proposed reply on Franklin engines if the final lines are omitted, arguing the US should not endorse export commodities.

subfiles.title: Western European Affairs routing note to Hornbeck
subfiles.about: Requests Hornbeck's comments on recommendations associated with the Franklin-engine case.
subfiles.summary: Largely illegible routing note asking Hornbeck's comment on the War Department memorandum that follows.

subfiles.title: War Department memorandum on Franklin engines for the Japanese Army
subfiles.to: Division of Western European Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Proposes allowing sales of Franklin engines or vehicles to the Japanese Army while withholding experimental plans and specifications.
subfiles.summary: War Department has no objection to selling Franklin engines or vehicles to Japan, but advises against supplying plans for experimental drive trucks; asks State's agreement.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing French arms exports
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Paris despatch about French infantry-armament exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Memo: the French War Minister admitted private industry exported infantry arms to the Far East in early 1932, answering a question on twenty tons of shells to Japan.

subfiles.title: Paris despatch on French sales of war matériel to Japan
subfiles.from: Theodore Marriner, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Reports a French ministerial response concerning private arms exports and alleged Hotchkiss-shell shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Paris: Deputy Doriot asked about twenty tons of Hotchkiss shells to Japan; the Minister admitted exports to China and Japan without denying the shipment, though trade returns showed none.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on British arms exports to China and Japan
subfiles.about: References a military attaché report on British arms exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to report 32933 on arms movements from Britain to both China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on reported Mauser shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: References testimony by a former Mauser employee alleging important firearms shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: a former Mauser Werke employee asserted arms shipments had gone to Japan.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Chinese criticism of French arms exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports Chinese newspaper allegations that French arms exports to Japan had increased sixfold since the occupation of Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Reuters from Nanking: Chinese papers denounce French arms sales to Japan, saying France effectively aids Japanese aggression.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on British arms-export licenses
subfiles.about: References official British figures on arms, ammunition, and military stores licensed for export to Japan and China.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: British arms export licenses for Japan and China in November 1932, presented to the Commons December 22.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Stimson's view of a bilateral munitions embargo
subfiles.about: Records Stimson's warning that an embargo on both China and Japan might hurt China without materially injuring Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Stimson told the British Ambassador that Japan could blockade anyway, so an equal embargo would help little and could disadvantage China.

subfiles.title: New York Herald Tribune clipping on alleged French arms sales
subfiles.from: United Press and New York Herald Tribune
subfiles.about: Reports an alleged eight-million-dollar Japanese arms contract with Hotchkiss and broader growth in French munitions exports.
subfiles.summary: Herald Tribune clipping: a reported $8 million Hotchkiss arms contract for Japan, which the Japanese Embassy called unlikely; also an Anti-Imperialist League demonstration at the Chinese Consulate.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting report of an alleged Japanese arms contract
subfiles.from: W. R. Castle Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Sends the American Ambassador in Paris a newspaper report about an alleged Japanese arms purchase from a French firm.
subfiles.summary: Castle sends the United Press story on the alleged Japanese arms contract, for possible interest rather than as verified.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on intensified Hamburg arms shipments
subfiles.about: References a despatch reporting increased shipments of war matériel from Hamburg to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Dominian's despatch on reported intensification of German-port arms traffic to Japan.

subfiles.title: Despatch on German-port shipments of war matériel to Japan
subfiles.from: Leon Dominian, American Consul General in charge
subfiles.about: Relays a communist newspaper's claims that numerous ships were carrying artillery, powder, and other war matériel from Hamburg to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Despatch: a German communist paper alleges intensified Hamburg shipments of artillery and powder to Japan on named vessels; unverified.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on the 1932 war-material export digest
subfiles.from: State Department, Division of Far Eastern Affairs (Langdon)
subfiles.about: References a digest of war-material exports to Japan during the first ten months of 1932.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Langdon's 1932 digest comparing war-material exports to China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Digest of war-material exports to China and Japan
subfiles.about: Tabulates American exports of arms, ammunition, aircraft, explosives, cotton, and linters to China and Japan during the first ten months of 1932.
subfiles.summary: Digest: listed military goods exports were $270,509 to China and $391,155 to Japan, with far larger raw cotton trade; aircraft via Hong Kong were for Canton.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on League interest in Far Eastern arms shipments
subfiles.about: References a Geneva telegram about British approaches to governments concerning arms shipments to the Far East.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: the League advisory committee was told Britain had contacted other governments and asked to be kept informed of arms shipments.

subfiles.title: Geneva telegram on the League Advisory Committee and arms shipments
subfiles.about: Reports the first meeting of the League committee created to follow the Sino-Japanese dispute.
subfiles.summary: The committee invited the United States and Russia to cooperate in its work under the Covenant. It learned that the British Government had approached interested governments about Far Eastern arms shipments and requested continuing information. Hymans presided as Assembly president, while selection of a permanent committee president was deferred.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on the Chinese view of an arms embargo
subfiles.about: References a Chinese Foreign Office argument that any arms embargo should apply only to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: a Chinese spokesman says China acts in self-defense, so equal restrictions would help the well-armed aggressor.

subfiles.title: Telegram reporting Chinese opposition to an equal arms embargo
subfiles.about: Transmits a Reuters report of the Chinese Foreign Office position that an embargo should be confined to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Telegram: China's spokesman says equal treatment of both states would be unjust and assist well-armed Japan.

subfiles.title: Duplicate cross-reference note on Stimson's munitions-embargo view
subfiles.about: Duplicates the record of Stimson's warning that an embargo on both China and Japan would operate unequally.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate cross-reference: Stimson believed an embargo would not injure Japan but might harm China, and Japan's navy could blockade.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on China's response to the British arms embargo
subfiles.about: References a Chinese Foreign Office statement that the embargo should be limited to Japan as the aggressor.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Johnson's telegram: China says an equal embargo contradicts the League's condemnation of Japan.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Chinese denunciation of the British arms embargo
subfiles.about: Reports official and press criticism in China of Britain's embargo on arms exports to both China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Foreign Office argued that the League's condemnation of Japanese aggression required restrictions to fall only on Japan. Because China produced few defensive weapons, an equal embargo would weaken Chinese resistance while facilitating Japanese operations. Chinese newspapers mocked British claims of friendliness and described John Simon's policy as effectively pro-Japanese.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on anticipated effects of the British embargo
subfiles.about: References a report that Britain's Far Eastern arms embargo would increase the power of Japanese military aggression.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Chinese expectation that the British embargo's equal restrictions would strengthen Japan's military advantage.
